title: Freddie Hubbard's cue and Marshall Royal's solo, with an Ellington lesson
summary: Jones tells how he coached Hubbard to play what he saw on screen and treated Marshall Royal like a vocalist; Parks heard Ellington in it.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: You were telling me, off the tape, when we had to stop a minute ago, about how you wrote the part that
And about the part that Marshall Royal played, Marshall's solo in the radio scene.

Well, this was a thing where I'd learned some things from Ellington, to put the human element in the -- into the person -- into the horn and to take the notes off the paper, because the notes cannot play. You have to have the interpretation, you know? And Freddie Hubbard was sitting Here's a great big, what, 40 pieces, I guess. there. (Unintelligible) And he had what we call a cue, a part to play, and Shaft was making love to this lady, and Freddie was playing it as a typical jazz solo, which he's very adept at doing, but that wasn't quite the thing that I wanted. He says, "What do you want me to play?" I said, Swivel "Swivle your chair around and look at the screen and see what Shaft is doing." And he was in the bedroom with this lady. I said, "Play that. Just play that, what you see." And fortunately enough his girl friend was there. So he did it. He did it very good. And on the Marshall Royal thing, I thought about Marshall for several days. I said, well, I better treat him right as an accompanist, which I've made my living at. But treat him as a vocalist, as though he's like Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan. Because he's in that echelon musically. I think he's a great musician. And he did what was necessary. But I would call him up and ask him all the registers of his

saxophone that he wanted to touch, didn't want to touch, or whatever. We just talked about it, you know, until I found out the key, or the style I wanted to do the accompaniment, you know. And it turned out very well.

That's very interesting. You say you took a lesson from Ellington in writing that, because at the screening of the picture Gordon came up to me at the end of the picture, and he said, "Did you hear that Ellington music?"
I don't -- see, now, I was so tired at that point, and really worn out from concentration, I didn't know Gordon was aware of that.
I didn't know, you know. I'm just doing what I know, that's all, you know. I'm glad that -- that's a positive compliment.
